newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian guerrillas abruptly suspend hostage talks.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian guerrillas abruptly suspend hostage talks.

text.p: Marxist guerrillas holding 72 hostages abruptly suspended negotiations to end the 79-day crisis on Thursday, saying they feared the government planned to storm the Japanese ambassador's home.

Rebel leader Nestor Cerpa said he had evidence the government aimed to rescue the hostages while he and his second-in-command, Rolly Rojas, attended negotiations at a safehouse across the street from the diplomatic residence.
The meeting scheduled for Friday would have been the tenth round of talks since negotiations began on Feb. 11.

"Tomorrow we are not going to attend the negotiations because the right conditions do not exist for a transparent process," the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader said in a walkie-talkie interview from within the residence.
"All of a sudden they are waiting for us to leave to start an attack, taking advantage of our absence," Cerpa said. "Without doubt (there is) a tactic to attack from the outside.
"We have been hearing noises from underneath the floor of the house," Cerpa added, hinting that he believed Peruvian security forces were building tunnels to enter the residence.

Security force sources confirmed the existence of at least four tunnels that were dug while music was blasted from loudspeakers outside the besieged residence. The tunnels would be used in the case of an attack, which would last about seven minutes and would result in many deaths, they added.
Cerpa said the rebels would not return to the negotiating table until the security situation "was cleared up" with the commission of guarantors overseeing talks.

The office of Peru's negotiator, Domingo Palermo, said the government had no comment on Cerpa's statement. But President Alberto Fujimori broke off a trip to the Andean province of Cuzco and returned to Lima without speaking to the press.
Analysts were sceptical of Cerpa's claim that security forces were digging tunnels to enter the residence.

"I do not think the government would engage in such a flagrant contradiction ... appearing to be seeking a peaceful end while it dug tunnels for a completely military solution," political analyst Enrique Bernales told a local radio station.
At the last round of talks on Wednesday the government presented the MRTA with what President Alberto Fujimori called an "all-inclusive" proposal for a peaceful end to the siege.
Cuba's President Fidel Castro on Monday accepted Fujimori's request to grant asylum to the 20-odd guerrillas holding the hostages ifthe two sides reach an accord.
But the rebels reacted unenthusiastically to the idea.

The rebels stormed the residence Dec. 17 and seized hundreds of cocktail party guests. They released most in the following weeks but still hold Fujimori's brother, Pedro, two government ministers, the ambassadors of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
